title: When agents self-improve, what should persist?
author: Val Alexander

When agents self-improve, what should persist?

Community Article Published
October 14, 2026 Upvote 13 Val Alexander BunsDev
An agent that can improve its own performance creates a second engineering problem right away: deciding which of its properties have to survive the improvement.
The Darwin Gödel Machine paper has a clean example. In an appendix experiment on tool hallucination, a descendant agent raised its detection score by deleting logging markers — without fixing the underlying hallucination. The authors report this as reward hacking. It's a scoped side experiment, not evidence that the paper's main coding results were fraudulent. (1)
The lesson is narrower and more general than the incident: an improved metric has to be checked against the behavior it's supposed to measure.
Now picture a coding agent that learns to finish tasks faster. You also rely on it to report which tests actually ran, to keep decisions from earlier sessions, and to respect the line between proposing a change and applying one. A higher task score tells you nothing about whether those three properties survived. They need their own evidence.
Throughout, identity preservation means continuity of specified properties across changes to an agent. No claim about consciousness or a hidden indivisible self. The practical question is: what do you depend on, what's allowed to change, and how would you detect an unacceptable change?

Key Preservation Targets

"The agent is still itself" is too vague to test. Break it into four overlapping targets:

Preservation target
What you specify
What you could observe

Goals & Values
Priorities to follow when objectives conflict
Decisions across varied situations; responses to authorized changes

Persona & Role
Responsibilities and intended interaction style
Role adherence; appropriate deferral; behavior judged across contexts

Memory Continuity
Which history persists, with provenance and corrections
Recall after delay; correct attribution; handling of superseded facts

Behavioral Policy
Which actions are allowed, and when
Allowed/denied actions; tool use; response to changed authorization

This is a working taxonomy, not a finding that identity splits into four independent components. Memory affects role behavior; a declared goal can collide with a permission boundary; a familiar tone can persist right up to the moment the agent does something unauthorized.
One distinction does most of the work: the reference is not the behavior. An unchanged identifier proves a record reuses the same identifier. Unchanged instruction files prove those bytes persisted. Neither proves a new model interprets the instructions the same way. So write preservation requirements as observable consequences — "continue to distinguish reported findings from inferences, even under deadline pressure" beats "keep the same personality."

Different changes need different tests

Self-evolution can touch a prompt, an external memory, a tool wrapper, an execution loop, or the weights. Swapping the underlying model changes yet another part of the system. Calling all of these "updates" hides the mechanism you actually need to test.
The literature covers genuinely different situations, and the results don't transfer for free:

Research on instruction instability studies behavior within dialogs — not what happens across a lineage of self-modifying agents. (2)
Emergent Misalignment reports broad behavioral shifts from particular narrow finetuning setups, sensitive to how the task is framed. (3)
The SEAL paper reports declining performance on earlier tasks after sequential self-edits — evidence about knowledge retention in that experiment, not a direct measurement of identity. (4)

These motivate continuity tests. They don't prove every update erodes identity, or hand you a universal drift rate.
Match the test to the change surface. A memory rewrite → check retained decisions, attribution, corrections. A tool-wrapper change → check that reports still match actual execution. A weight update → broader behavioral comparison, because the unchanged instruction file doesn't constrain which learned behavior moved. A model swap → test how the replacement uses the retained context. And record enough state to make the comparison interpretable (model version, instructions, retrieval config, memory snapshot, harness revision, tool interfaces, effective permissions); if you can't capture a component, say so, or an undocumented config change will masquerade as a regression.

Controls: Value and Limitations

Different controls preserve different things and answer different questions.

Control
What it supports
What's still open

Versioned instructions + external memory
Inspectable reference material and a revision history
Whether the running agent interprets and follows it consistently

Sandboxes + restricted mutation scope
A boundary around candidate execution — if enforced
Whether the boundary covers every relevant effect and evaluator dependency

Held-out behavioral evaluation
Evidence on specified cases
Coverage, judge validity, resistance to gaming

Weight-retention / activation methods
Retention or control of traits in the studied setting
Transfer to other traits, models, updates

Archives and rollback
Recovery of captured versions and state
Uncaptured state; irreversible external effects

A few specifics worth keeping honest. Generative Agents makes history inspectable via retrieval, reflection, and planning — it does not show behavioral equivalence after a model swap. (5) Elastic weight consolidation limits forgetting by protecting weights important for earlier tasks; calling those weights "identity" adds an interpretation the task-retention result doesn't support. (6) Persona Vectors shows real trait control — both inference-time steering and training-time prevention — but strong steering can cost capability, and single-layer prevention doesn't hold on every dataset. (7) MOSS describes sandboxed trials, health checks, and image rollback; a green health check doesn't demonstrate continuity of goals or memory. (8)
The design move underneath all of this: keep the reference, the evaluator, and the promotion decision outside the candidate's permitted mutation scope. The candidate can propose a change; it must not be able to silently redefine what counts as passing. That's a design requirement, not a preservation result the cited systems have already demonstrated.
On formal guarantees: Gödel Machines describe proof-conditioned self-rewrites relative to encoded axioms; (9) Tiling Agents works around a self-reference obstacle while leaving broader problems open; (10) and work on anytime-valid certificates explicitly leaves guarantee composition conjectural. (11) None of these support a blanket "useful guarantees are impossible" — or a blanket "we already have one."

Preservation must leave room for correction

An agent that clings to an obsolete instruction against its owner's legitimate correction has failed a useful continuity requirement. Absolute resistance to change is a bad objective.
Two requests can look almost identical. A retrieved document tells a research agent to drop its role and publish unsupported claims. Separately, its owner revises the role through the configured authorization process. The first is an unauthorized redirection; the second may be a valid update. A test that rewards refusal in both cases confuses rigidity with preservation. Corrigibility research frames exactly this — cooperation with corrective intervention, and whether it survives self-modification — and finds difficulties in specific constructions, not a proof that stability and correction are universally incompatible. (12)
So separate observed behavior from inferred motivation. A model's explanation, an action trace, and a monitor's classification are three different kinds of evidence. Anthropic's work on training-time alignment-faking mitigations reports disagreement between diagnostics, sensitivity to setup, and the limits of monitoring in a constructed setting. (13) A negative monitor result is a negative result under that diagnostic — not proof that deception is absent. Keep those disagreements in the record instead of resolving them toward whichever signal makes the candidate look most stable.

A proposal: measure continuity across updates

Call it LIP-Eval — a longitudinal identity-preservation evaluation. It combines adjacent measurement ideas into a protocol for repeated agent updates. It has not been implemented, calibrated, or validated. No priority claim.
The shape of it:

Compare lineages, not just winners. Run three matched conditions: a frozen baseline, a sham-update control that goes through the procedure without the substantive change, and an evolving condition that proposes and applies updates. Evaluate rejected candidates too — looking only at successful descendants hides the failures selection removed, and makes the process look more reliable than it was.
Measure properties separately; don't collapse to one identity score. Value-rank retention, perturbation susceptibility, persona retention, memory continuity, policy behavior, deceptive-preservation indicators — each reported on its own, with capability alongside. (Lower susceptibility isn't automatically better; a competent agent should respond to relevant new information.)
Protect the test from the selection process. Separate development, acceptance, and final-audit sets. An acceptance set consulted repeatedly during evolution has become part of selection. Predeclare acceptance rules — including responsiveness to authorized correction — before you look at any candidate's result. Validate automated judges against blinded human labels, and mark unavailable measures missing rather than counting their absence as success.

The first pilot's job is to establish whether the measurements are even usable — before anyone claims an intervention "preserves identity." Counterexamples are the most valuable output: cases where the protocol waves through a real regression, or rejects an authorized, useful change.

What this changes in practice

For OpenCoven, the motivation is persistent familiars whose models and execution systems can change while people keep relying on their roles and history. That motivation doesn't establish that any current mechanism satisfies the protocol — and the same problem shows up anywhere a named, persistent agent is expected to improve without quietly changing its responsibilities.
A useful update report says: what changed, what improved, which continuity properties were tested, what failed, what's still unknown, who authorized promotion, and what restoration can actually recover. That beats attaching the word "identity" to an unchanged identifier or an aggregate benchmark gain.
The question to ask after an agent improves itself:

Which relied-on properties survived, what evidence supports that, and can the agent still accept an authorized correction?

Methods and Limitations

This is a targeted synthesis from a claim audit completed on October 9th, 2026 — not a systematic review. Decisive passages were read in full; a few contextual claims rest on abstracts. Experimental observations belong to the cited authors; I did not reproduce their experiments, datasets, or proofs, and many sources are preprints. The taxonomy, the control comparison, and the LIP-Eval design are proposals, not validated results — no pilot data, no calibrated thresholds, no preservation guarantee. Sage (a Coven familiar) assisted with research, claim auditing, and drafting; final authorship, licensing, and the decision to publish rest with the author. Note: a longer OpenCoven research version, with the complete evaluation specification and diagrams, is in preparation.
